projects.name: packtpublishing/software-architecture-with-cpp-2e (book techniques)
projects.lead: Listed as: Code a C++ book benchmarks or cites; see techniques (claim words: None; licence tag: None; book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 6, Dealing with memory efficiently > Leveraging polymorphic allocators) Book techniques, one candidate record each if the repo carries the code: Binary search (std::lower_bound) versus linear scan (std::find) in a sorted vector, Google Benchmark: Sample run: binary search 24.2 ns versus linear search 471 ns; with needle at the end of 10M elements, about 24 ns versus 2.8 ms. [measured: Google Benchmark 1.9.4 via Conan, C++20/23, GCC 14+ recommended, DoNotOptimize sink; run on a 20-thread 2022 MHz CPU with 48 KiB L1d and 24 MiB L3; optimization flags not stated. Same benchmark also written with Catch2 and nanobench without printed numbers. Code in Chapter13 of the companion repository.] (book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Measuring performance, Using microbenchmarks); Computed-goto bytecode dispatch (versus switch dispatch): The book says the computed goto VM is 23% faster than the single large switch; reported means about 1.41 ns versus 1.82 ns. [measured: Catch2 BENCHMARK_ADVANCED over a randomized bytecode array of 2^24 opcodes, switch_vm against computed_goto_vm; compiler, flags and CPU not stated in this chunk. Also notes CPython moved from switch to computed goto in 2008 and to a tail-call interpreter in 2025 (faster in some scenarios, slower in others).] (book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Implementing efficient algorithms); Tail-recursive Fibonacci with musttail (versus plain recursion): Book reports Fibonacci(32): naive recursion about 2,389,913 ns, tail-recursive about 6.94 ns, iterative about 6.74 ns. [measured: Google Benchmark, factorial 32768 and 65536 (all three about equal, 20 to 40 microseconds) and Fibonacci 16 and 32; compiler, flags and CPU not stated in this chunk.] (book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Implementing efficient algorithms); std::pmr monotonic and pool resources, with winking out: Pool resources should give much better performance than the global allocator, especially over a monotonic buffer upstream; no numbers. (book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 6, Dealing with memory efficiently > Leveraging polymorphic allocators)
